summary: Region decides the differential. The neck packs airway, vascular, and aerodigestive structures into a small space — hard signs go straight to the OR, soft signs get CT angiography. The chest has two immediately treatable causes of obstructive shock that should not wait for imaging. The mangled extremity forces the salvage-versus-amputation question before full imaging, and MESS is better at identifying salvageable limbs than at mandating amputation.
whyThisMatters: A small entry wound over the neck or chest can carry a large, time-critical differential, and the decisions that matter — operate now versus image, decompress versus wait, salvage versus amputate — are made in the first minutes on physical findings, before CT. Knowing which findings force which action is what keeps a survivable injury survivable.
clinicalTakeaway: Neck: hard signs (shock, pulsatile bleeding or expanding hematoma, bruit/thrill, pulse deficit with neuro change) mandate immediate operative exploration — do not delay for imaging; soft signs or platysma violation in a stable patient get CT angiography, with a low threshold for esophagoscopy/bronchoscopy since CTA is less reliable for aerodigestive injury. Chest: treat tension pneumothorax and tamponade as clinical diagnoses in the unstable patient — needle/finger decompression, and for a cardiac-box wound with shock, resuscitative thoracotomy. Extremity: use MESS to support salvage in a low-scoring limb rather than to mandate amputation on a high score; blast/crush mechanism, polytrauma, and massive transfusion independently raise amputation rates.

body.text: The neck concentrates airway, vascular, and aerodigestive structures with minimal protection. It is historically divided into three zones to guide surgical versus selective management, though a track can cross zones and the "no zone" approach (CTA-driven regardless of zone) has gained favor at many centers.

rows: Zone I
Clavicles / thoracic inlet to cricoid cartilage
High risk of occult vascular or thoracic injury; may need sternotomy or thoracic surgical involvement; endovascular options considered early
Zone II
Cricoid cartilage to angle of the mandible
Most accessible surgically; historically explored directly, though CTA has reduced negative explorations here too
Zone III
Angle of the mandible to skull base
High risk of occult vascular injury; surgically difficult — endovascular management often preferred
Hard signs
Shock; pulsatile bleeding or expanding hematoma; audible bruit / palpable thrill; pulse loss with a stable or evolving neurologic deficit
Immediate operative exploration or urgent definitive intervention — do not delay for imaging
Soft signs
Stable non-expanding hematoma; minor hemoptysis or hematemesis; dysphonia or dysphagia; subcutaneous or mediastinal air; bleeding at the scene
CT angiography (or duplex) in the stable patient rather than immediate exploration

items: Platysma violation raises the likelihood of deep-structure injury and generally warrants workup even without hard or soft signs.
CTA sensitivity for major vascular injury is ~90-100% and is the default screen in stable patients with soft signs or proximity findings.

Physical exam is highly sensitive for vascular injury but less reliable for aerodigestive injury — keep a low threshold for esophagoscopy, esophagography, or bronchoscopy when aerodigestive injury is suspected despite a negative CTA.

body.text: Two immediately treatable causes of obstructive shock from penetrating (and sometimes blunt) chest trauma — both clinical diagnoses that should not wait for imaging in an unstable patient.

items: Tension pneumothorax: hypotension, absent/decreased unilateral breath sounds, distended neck veins, often tracheal deviation away from the affected side. Treatment: immediate needle or finger decompression, then tube thoracostomy.

Pericardial tamponade (penetrating cardiac wound): hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad, often incomplete). In a penetrating chest wound with cardiac-box involvement and shock, resuscitative thoracotomy or emergent pericardiocentesis / sternotomy may be the only interventions fast enough to matter.

body.text: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta is a bridge to definitive hemostasis for non-compressible torso or junctional hemorrhage — preserving cerebral and cardiac perfusion while surgical or interventional control is arranged.

rows: Zone I
Descending thoracic aorta — left subclavian to celiac artery
Suspected intra-abdominal or thoracic hemorrhage, profound shock, or impending collapse; preserves brain and heart perfusion at the cost of increased LV afterload
Zone II
Paravisceral aorta — celiac to lowest renal artery
Avoided — severe visceral / renal ischemia risk with no compensating benefit over Zone I or III
Zone III
Infrarenal aorta — lowest renal artery to bifurcation
Pelvic fracture or junctional femoral / groin hemorrhage without suspected thoraco-abdominal injury; more modest hemodynamic effect than Zone I

body.text: Ballistic and blast trauma to an extremity raises the salvage-versus-amputation question early, often before full imaging. The Mangled Extremity Severity Score (MESS) is the most widely applied bedside tool, though its predictive value is better established for identifying salvageable limbs (low score) than for mandating amputation on a high score.

rows: Skeletal / soft-tissue injury
Graded 1-4 from low energy (stab, simple fracture) to high energy or mass-casualty crush/blast with gross contamination
Limb ischemia
Graded 1-3 (doubled if ischemia duration > 6 h), from a pulse-reduced but perfused limb to a pulseless, cool, paralyzed, insensate limb
Shock
Graded 0-2 from normotensive to persistent field or arrival hypotension
Age
Graded 0-2, increasing with age given lower physiologic reserve

body.text: A MESS of 7 or higher is the most commonly cited amputation-associated cutoff, but multiple validation studies (including combat casualty data) show only modest sensitivity for this threshold and caution against using it as an automatic indication. The decision remains clinical — weighing mechanism, ischemia time, associated injuries, and reconstructive resources. Blast and crush mechanisms, polytrauma, and massive-transfusion requirement are independently associated with higher amputation rates even where MESS performs imperfectly as a predictor.
